lead: A fuselage or wing must carry loads and keep its shape. Three classic arrangements do this: a truss of bars covered with fabric, a monocoque where the skin alone carries everything, and a semi-monocoque where the skin works with a skeleton. The semi-monocoque wins for modern aircraft because it lets the skin stay thin while stringers and longerons take bending. Only a few universities examine this as a separate topic, but the names appear in every structural description.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the names of the members, and the idea of a load path.

blocks.text: A truss fuselage is a frame of metal tubes with diagonal wires and fabric covering. The tubes carry the flight loads; the fabric mainly keeps the air out. The truss is light for small aircraft but poor for pressurisation, because a pressure cabin needs a sealed shell, not a fabric bag.

A monocoque shell is different. The skin alone carries bending, shear, torsion and pressure, with no stringer-and-frame skeleton. A pure monocoque is simple but heavy. A thin unstiffened shell buckles at low compression, so the skin must be thick enough to resist buckling. Thick skin adds weight.

A semi-monocoque shell puts a skeleton back under a thin skin. Skin, stringers, longerons and frames share the load. This is the usual construction for modern transport fuselages and many wings. Typical wing and fuselage arrangements are in Chapter 1.3.

In a semi-monocoque fuselage the skin is a thin sheet of aluminium alloy or composite. It carries shear, torsion and all the cabin pressure. Stringers are small longitudinal members riveted to the skin. They stiffen the skin and share the bending. Longerons are the few large longitudinal members that carry most of the bending, especially near doors and cut-outs. Frames are rings around the fuselage. They hold the cross-section in shape and shorten the skin panels so each panel can resist buckling.

Pressure is the clearest load. Treat a pressurised fuselage as a thin cylinder. Let p be the cabin differential pressure in Pa, r the radius in m and t the skin thickness in m. Buckling of the stiffened panels is left to Unit 6, Plates, Buckling and Composite Structures.

blocks.where: σh is hoop stress in Pa; p is differential pressure in Pa; r is radius in m; t is skin thickness in m.
σl is longitudinal stress in Pa; the symbols are the same.

blocks.text: The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress. Hoop stress comes from pressure pushing sideways on a split cylinder. Longitudinal stress comes from pressure on the end caps.

figure.caption: Three construction types side by side. In the semi-monocoque branch, notice that the skin keeps pressure while stringers and frames have separate jobs.

spec.aria: A tree shows truss, monocoque and semi-monocoque construction, with the semi-monocoque branch split into skin, stringers and frames.

examples.question: A semi-monocoque fuselage has a circular cross-section of diameter 2.0 m and skin thickness 1.5 mm. The cabin differential pressure is 60 kPa. Find the hoop and longitudinal stresses in the skin.
steps: Diameter D = 2.0 m, so radius r = D/2 = 1.0 m. Thickness t = 1.5 mm = 0.0015 m. Pressure p = 60 kPa = 60 000 Pa.
Longitudinal stress: σl = pr/(2t) = σh/2 = 20 000 000 Pa = 20 MPa.
examples.answer: The hoop stress is 40 MPa and the longitudinal stress is 20 MPa.
examples.check:
p = 60000.0
r = 1.0
t = 0.0015
hoop = p * r / t / 1e6
longitudinal = hoop / 2
print(int(round(hoop)))
print(int(round(longitudinal)))

traps: Do not say the stringers carry the cabin pressure. The skin is the pressure membrane; stringers only stiffen it.
Do not swap hoop and longitudinal stress. Hoop stress pr/t is twice longitudinal pr/2t.
Do not use diameter in place of radius. For a 2.0 m fuselage, r = 1.0 m.
Do not leave kPa or mm in the formula. Convert 60 kPa to 60 000 Pa and 1.5 mm to 0.0015 m.
Do not call any stiffened shell a monocoque. A pure monocoque has no stringer-and-frame skeleton carrying bending.

quiz.a: A shell where the skin carries all structural loads, with no separate stringer-and-frame skeleton.

quiz.q: Why is a pure monocoque heavy?
quiz.a: A thin unstiffened skin buckles; making it thick enough to resist buckling adds weight.

quiz.q: State one job each of skin, stringers and frames.
quiz.a: Skin carries shear and pressure; stringers carry bending and stiffen the skin; frames hold shape and shorten panels.

quiz.q: A thin cylinder has r = 0.8 m, t = 2.0 mm and p = 50 kPa. Find hoop stress.
A student says the semi-monocoque skin carries no load because stringers are present. Correct it.
quiz.a: The skin still carries all cabin pressure and shear. Stringers help with bending and stiffening but do not seal the cabin.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, semi-monocoque sizing is done with finite element models that couple skin, stringers and frames. Fatigue cracks often start at rivet holes in the skin, so the pressure membrane is inspected regularly. Newer composite fuselages use large co-cured shells with integrated stringers, which is a semi-monocoque idea in one piece. Search next for stiffened panel buckling and fuselage pressure membrane.
